outline: Identify the reaction by what changes: addition, substitution, elimination, hydrolysis, condensation or redox. Follow electron movement to classify the mechanism. Homolysis creates radicals; heterolysis creates ions. Nucleophiles donate electron pairs and electrophiles accept them. In a full curly-arrow mechanism, every arrow begins at the source bond or lone pair.

misconceptions.refutation: Each atom receives one bonding electron, forming radicals; heterolytic fission produces ions.
misconceptions.contrast: Homolytic: one electron each. Heterolytic: both electrons to one atom.

misconceptions.refutation: A neutral molecule with a lone pair, such as ammonia, can donate that pair.
misconceptions.contrast: Electron-pair donation defines a nucleophile, not charge.

misconceptions.statement: A curly arrow can start at an electrophilic atom.
misconceptions.refutation: A full curly arrow traces an electron pair from its source: a bond or lone pair.
misconceptions.contrast: Start at the electron pair and point towards its destination.

misconceptions.refutation: The carbon nucleophile attacks the carbonyl carbon while the C=O pair moves to oxygen, giving an alkoxide.
misconceptions.contrast: Show the C=O polarity and arrows from the cyanide lone pair and C=O bond.

flashcards.back: A family of organic compounds with the same functional group and general formula; successive members differ by $\ce{CH2}$.
Saturated: contains only carbon–carbon single bonds. Unsaturated: contains a carbon–carbon double or triple bond.
Homolytic: each atom receives one electron from the bond, forming radicals. Heterolytic: one atom receives both bonding electrons, forming ions.
A species with an unpaired electron.
A nucleophile donates an electron pair; an electrophile accepts an electron pair.
Addition combines reactants into one product; substitution replaces an atom or group; elimination removes atoms or groups, usually forming a multiple bond.
Hydrolysis breaks a bond by reaction with water. Condensation joins molecules with loss of a small molecule, often water.
Oxidation is gain of oxygen or loss of hydrogen; reduction is loss of oxygen or gain of hydrogen. $[O]$ and $[H]$ each represent one atom supplied by the appropriate reagent.

9701-13.2.1.motivate: Reaction names become useful when they tell you exactly what changes in bonds or electrons. The same short vocabulary works across the organic syllabus.
9701-13.2.1.establish: A homologous series has the same functional group and general formula; successive members differ by $\ce{CH2}$. Saturated compounds have only carbon–carbon single bonds; unsaturated compounds have a carbon–carbon multiple bond. Homolytic fission gives one bonding electron to each atom, forming free radicals with unpaired electrons. Heterolytic fission gives both electrons to one atom, forming ions. Radical initiation generates radicals, propagation consumes and regenerates radicals, and termination removes radicals by combination. A nucleophile donates an electron pair; an electrophile accepts one. Addition combines reactants into one product; substitution replaces an atom or group; elimination removes atoms or groups, often forming a multiple bond. Hydrolysis breaks a bond using water; condensation joins molecules with loss of a small molecule. Organic oxidation is gain of oxygen or loss of hydrogen, and reduction is loss of oxygen or gain of hydrogen. $[O]$ and $[H]$ represent one atom of oxygen from an oxidising agent and one atom of hydrogen from a reducing agent, respectively.
9701-13.2.1.connect: Electron-pair donors are nucleophiles; electron-pair acceptors are electrophiles. This links the reaction labels here to the four mechanism types in the next idea.
9701-13.2.1.note:
- Homolysis → radicals; heterolysis → ions.
- Initiation creates, propagation sustains, termination removes radicals.
- Addition joins; substitution replaces; elimination removes.
- Hydrolysis uses water; condensation loses a small molecule.
- Oxidation gains O or loses H; reduction loses O or gains H.

options.A: Both bonding electrons move to one atom.
options.B: Each bonded atom receives one electron.
options.C: An electron pair moves from a lone pair to carbon.
options.D: A bond breaks by reaction with water.

discover.explanation: Equal division of the bonding pair forms two radicals.

9701-13.2.2.motivate: A mechanism explains a reaction at electron level. Its name predicts both the attacking species and the overall bond change.
9701-13.2.2.establish: Free-radical substitution replaces an atom through radical initiation, propagation and termination; alkane chlorination under UV light is an example. Electrophilic addition begins when an alkene π bond donates a pair to an electrophile; addition across $\ce{C=C}$ follows. Nucleophilic substitution begins when a nucleophile donates a lone pair to a carbon attached to a leaving group, which departs; cyanide replacing bromide is an example. Nucleophilic addition begins when a nucleophile donates a lone pair to the partially positive carbonyl carbon; the $\ce{C=O}$ pair moves to oxygen, and the alkoxide can then be protonated. Full curly arrows represent movement of electron pairs, so each arrow must start at the source bond or lone pair and point to the destination. Show relevant bond polarity and charges. A radical step instead transfers single electrons and uses single-headed arrows when drawn.
9701-13.2.2.connect: Use the terminology from the first idea to identify electron donors and acceptors, then ask whether the overall change is addition or substitution.
9701-13.2.2.note:
- Radical substitution: initiation, propagation, termination.
- Electrophilic addition: alkene π bond attacks electrophile.
- Nucleophilic substitution: lone-pair donor replaces leaving group.
- Nucleophilic addition: donor attacks carbonyl carbon; $\ce{C=O}$ pair moves to oxygen.
- Full curly arrows start at a bond or lone pair.

options.A: At the atom receiving an electron pair.

discover.explanation: The tail identifies the electron-pair source; the head shows where the pair moves.
